title: JavaScript
description: Learn to program with JavaScript, the language of the web: from your first line of output to classes, recursion, and sorting and searching algorithms with complexity analysis.

js-01.title: Hello, world!
js-01.theory:
# Your first program

A program is a list of **instructions** that the computer runs one after another, from top to bottom. In JavaScript, the simplest instruction to show something on the screen is `console.log`:

```javascript
console.log("Olá, mundo!");
```

(`Olá, mundo!` is Portuguese for "Hello, world!"; the exercises in this track print their messages in Portuguese.)

The text between quotes is a **string** (a sequence of characters). You can use double quotes `"..."`, single quotes `'...'` or backticks `` `...` ``. Each call to `console.log` writes **one line** and moves on to the next.

```javascript
console.log("First line");
console.log("Second line");
```

## Why the semicolon?

The `;` marks the end of an instruction. JavaScript can usually guess where an instruction ends, but writing the `;` makes the code clearer and avoids surprises. We will always use it.

## Building text

With backticks you create a **template literal**: text that accepts values inside `${...}`. This will be very useful from now on:

```javascript
const nome = "Ana";
console.log(`Welcome, ${nome}!`);
```

(`nome` means "name"; we keep the variable names used in the exercise code.)

## Reading a line

In this track, programs receive data through **standard input**. The `prompt()` function (called **with no arguments**) returns the next line typed, as text. We will look at this carefully in lesson 3; for now, it's enough to know that:

```javascript
const nome = prompt();
console.log(`Hi, ${nome}!`);
```

## Common mistakes

- Forgetting to close the quotes or the parentheses: the program doesn't even start running (syntax error).
- Writing `Console.log` with a capital C: JavaScript is case-sensitive.
- Printing a message different from the one asked for: the grader compares the output **exactly**, letter by letter (spaces at the end of a line are ignored).
js-01.task:
Read a name (one line) and print exactly these three lines:

```
Olá, mundo!
Meu nome é <name>.
Estou aprendendo JavaScript!
```

(In English: "Hello, world!", "My name is <name>." and "I'm learning JavaScript!". The output must stay in Portuguese, exactly as shown.)

Example: for the input `Ana`, the output is:

```
Olá, mundo!
Meu nome é Ana.
Estou aprendendo JavaScript!
```
hints: Each line of the output is one call to console.log.
Use a template literal with backticks: `Meu nome é ${nome}.`
Check the period after the name and the accent on "é".

js-02.title: Variables and types
js-02.theory:
# Storing values

In lesson 1 you already used `const nome = prompt();`. This creates a **variable**: a name that points to a value stored in memory. In modern JavaScript there are two ways to create variables:

```javascript
const pi = 3.14;     // cannot be reassigned
let counter = 0;     // can change later
counter = counter + 1;
```

Prefer `const` and use `let` only when the value really needs to change. This keeps you from changing something by accident. (There is also the old `var`, which has confusing scope rules; avoid it.)

## Data types

Every value has a **type**. The main ones are:

- `string`: text, such as `"banana"`.
- `number`: numbers, whole or with decimal places (`42`, `-3.5`). JavaScript uses a single type for both.
- `boolean`: `true` or `false`.
- `null` and `undefined`: represent "no value".

The `typeof` operator tells you the type of a value:

```javascript
console.log(typeof "hi");   // string
console.log(typeof 42);     // number
console.log(typeof true);   // boolean
```

## Strings are also useful objects

Strings have **properties** and **methods**. `length` gives the number of characters; `toUpperCase()` and `toLowerCase()` return a new string in uppercase or lowercase; `at(-1)` gets the last character:

```javascript
const fruit = "banana";
console.log(fruit.length);        // 6
console.log(fruit.toUpperCase()); // BANANA
console.log(fruit.at(-1));        // a
console.log(fruit[0]);            // b
```

Note that the methods **do not change** the original string: strings in JavaScript are **immutable**. `fruit.toUpperCase()` creates a new text.

## Why do types matter?

The same operator does different things depending on the type. `+` adds numbers, but **concatenates** (joins) strings:

```javascript
console.log(2 + 3);     // 5
console.log("2" + "3"); // 23
```

This detail causes many bugs, which is why the next lesson explains how to convert text into a number.

## Common mistakes

- Trying to reassign a `const`: you get a `TypeError`.
- Writing `fruit.length()`: `length` is a property, with no parentheses.
- Thinking that `toUpperCase()` changes the variable: it returns a new string.
js-02.task:
Read a word (one line) and print four lines, exactly in this format:

```
Texto: <word>
Tamanho: <number of characters>
Maiúsculas: <word in uppercase>
Tipo: <result of typeof on the word>
```

(The labels are Portuguese for "Text", "Length", "Uppercase" and "Type"; keep them exactly as shown.)

Example: for the input `banana`:

```
Texto: banana
Tamanho: 6
Maiúsculas: BANANA
Tipo: string
```
hints: The number of characters is in the length property (no parentheses).
toUpperCase() returns a new string in uppercase.
typeof palavra returns the name of the type as text.

js-03.title: Input and arithmetic
js-03.theory:
# Reading data and doing math

## How the input arrives

Each exercise is checked by an **automatic grader**. It runs your program several times and, in each run, **types by itself** the input lines of the test. You don't need to (and shouldn't) show messages like "Enter a number": the grader compares **all** of the output with the expected output, and any extra text makes the test fail.

To read, use `prompt()` **with no arguments**. Each call returns the **next line** of the input as a **string**, or `null` when the input has run out. `readline()` does the same thing.

```javascript
const a = prompt(); // first line
const b = prompt(); // second line
```

## The problem with text

Remember lesson 2? `+` concatenates strings. So:

```javascript
const a = prompt(); // "2"
const b = prompt(); // "3"
console.log(a + b); // 23  (!)
```

You need to **convert** the text into a number:

- `Number("42")` gives `42`; `Number("3.5")` gives `3.5`; `Number("abc")` gives `NaN` ("not a number").
- `parseInt("42", 10)` reads an integer in base 10, stopping at the first invalid character: `parseInt("42abc", 10)` gives `42`.
- `parseFloat("3.5")` reads a number with decimal places.

Use `Number` when the whole line must be a number; always pass base `10` to `parseInt`.

## Arithmetic operators

```javascript
console.log(7 + 2);  // 9
console.log(7 - 2);  // 5
console.log(7 * 2);  // 14
console.log(7 / 2);  // 3.5   (division keeps the decimal part)
console.log(7 % 2);  // 1     (remainder)
console.log(2 ** 3); // 8     (power)
```

For **integer division**, use `Math.trunc(a / b)`, which cuts off the decimal part toward zero. With negatives, `Math.trunc(-7 / 2)` gives `-3`, and the remainder `-7 % 2` gives `-1`: in JavaScript the remainder has the **sign of the dividend**. (`Math.floor` rounds down and would give `-4`; they are different things!)

## Decimal places

Numbers with a fractional part can come out with many decimal places (`0.1 + 0.2` gives `0.30000000000000004`, because of the binary representation). To show a value with a fixed number of decimal places, use `toFixed`:

```javascript
const average = 7 / 2;
console.log(average.toFixed(2)); // 3.50
```

`toFixed` returns a **string** with a dot as the decimal separator.

## Common mistakes

- Forgetting to convert and getting `"23"` instead of `5`.
- Using `Math.floor` when the task asks you to truncate.
- Printing "enter..." messages before reading.
js-03.task:
Read two integers `a` and `b` (one per line; `b` is never zero) and print:

```
Soma: <a + b>
Diferença: <a - b>
Produto: <a * b>
Divisão inteira: <a / b truncated toward zero>
Resto: <a % b>
Média: <(a + b) / 2 with 2 decimal places>
```

(The labels mean Sum, Difference, Product, Integer division, Remainder and Average; keep them exactly in Portuguese.)

Example: for `7` and `2`:

```
Soma: 9
Diferença: 5
Produto: 14
Divisão inteira: 3
Resto: 1
Média: 4.50
```
hints: prompt() returns text: use Number(prompt()) to get a number.
Math.trunc(a / b) does integer division, truncating toward zero.
For the average, use ((a + b) / 2).toFixed(2).

js-05.title: Loops
js-05.task:
Read an integer `n` (n ≥ 0) and then `n` integers, one per line. Print:

```
Soma: <sum>
Maior: <largest value>
Menor: <smallest value>
```

(Soma = sum, Maior = largest, Menor = smallest.)

If `n` is 0, print only the line `Nenhum número` ("no numbers").

Example: for the input `3`, `4`, `-2`, `9`:

```
Soma: 11
Maior: 9
Menor: -2
```
hints: Use a for loop from 0 to n - 1 and read one number in each round.
Start the largest at -Infinity and the smallest at Infinity.
Handle n === 0 before the loop.

js-06.title: Functions
js-06.task:
Write a function `ehPrimo(n)` (isPrime) that returns `true` if `n` is prime and `false` otherwise. Then read two integers `a` and `b` (a ≤ b) and print, on a single line separated by spaces, all the primes in the closed interval `[a, b]` in increasing order. If there are none, print `Nenhum primo` ("no primes").

Example: for `10` and `20`, the output is:

```
11 13 17 19
```
hints: Numbers less than 2 are not prime.
Test divisors d starting at 2 while d * d <= n; if n % d === 0, it is not prime.

js-07.title: Arrays and strings
js-07.theory:
# Collections of values

An **array** stores several values in order, accessed by **index** starting at 0:

```javascript
const colors = ["blue", "green", "purple"];
console.log(colors[0]);      // blue
console.log(colors.length);  // 3
console.log(colors.at(-1));  // purple
colors.push("black");        // adds to the end
```

Unlike strings (lesson 2), arrays are **mutable**: `push`, `pop` and assignments like `colors[1] = "pink"` change the array itself. Even when it is declared with `const`, its contents can change; what `const` prevents is the variable pointing to another array (`colors = []` gives an error).

## Going through an array

```javascript
for (const color of colors) {
  console.log(color);
}
```

The `for...of` loop goes through each element. If you need the index, use the classic `for` from lesson 5.

## Methods that return something new

- `map(f)`: a new array with `f` applied to each item.
- `filter(f)`: a new array with only the items for which `f` gives `true`.
- `reverse()`: reverses **in place** (it changes the array!). To avoid changing it, copy it first: `[...arr].reverse()`.
- `join(sep)`: joins everything into a string.

```javascript
const nums = [1, 2, 3, 4];
const evens = nums.filter((n) => n % 2 === 0);
console.log(evens.join(", ")); // 2, 4
```

## From string to array and back

`split` breaks a string into an array; `join` does the opposite. This is the bridge between reading a line and working with its words (`palavras` means "words"):

```javascript
const sentence = "  the rat   ran ";
const palavras = sentence.trim().split(/\s+/);
```

`trim()` removes the spaces at both ends and `split(/\s+/)` splits on **one or more** spaces (a regular expression). Watch out: `"".split(/\s+/)` returns `[""]`, an array with **one** empty string, not an empty array! So handle the empty line separately, or filter: `.filter((p) => p !== "")`.

## Empty or missing line

If the input has no lines at all, `prompt()` returns `null`. The `??` operator provides a default value in that case: `const linha = prompt() ?? "";` (`linha` means "line").

## Common mistakes

- Printing the array with `console.log(arr)`: use `join` to control the format.
- Accessing `arr[arr.length]`, which is `undefined` (the last index is `length - 1`).
- Forgetting that `reverse()` changes the original array.
js-07.task:
Read a line with a sentence (the words may be separated by several spaces, and the line may be empty). Print:

```
Palavras: <number of words>
Invertida: <the words in reverse order, separated by one space>
Mais longa: <the longest word; in case of a tie, the one that appears first>
```

(Palavras = words, Invertida = reversed, Mais longa = longest; keep the labels in Portuguese.)

If there are no words, print only `Palavras: 0`.

Example: for `o rato roeu a roupa`:

```
Palavras: 5
Invertida: roupa a roeu rato o
Mais longa: roupa
```
hints: Use trim() and split(/\s+/), then filter out the empty strings.
To reverse without changing the original: [...palavras].reverse().join(" ").
When looking for the longest word, replace it only when the length is strictly greater (>), so the first one is kept in case of a tie.

js-08.title: Objects and classes
js-08.task:
Create a class `ContaBancaria` (BankAccount) with:

- `constructor(titular)` (`titular` = account holder): initial balance 0;
- `depositar(valor)` (deposit): adds to the balance;
- `sacar(valor)` (withdraw): if there is enough balance, subtracts and returns `true`; otherwise, changes nothing and returns `false`;
- a getter or method to check the balance (`saldo`).

Input: the account holder's name; then an integer `n`; then `n` lines, each one `D <amount>` (deposit) or `S <amount>` (withdrawal), with amounts that may have decimals.

For each operation print one line (amounts with 2 decimal places):

- `Depósito de <amount>` ("deposit of")
- `Saque de <amount>` ("withdrawal of") if it worked, or `Saldo insuficiente para sacar <amount>` ("insufficient balance to withdraw")

At the end: `Saldo de <account holder>: <balance>` ("balance of").

Example: for `Ana`, `3`, `D 100`, `S 30.5`, `S 200`:

```
Depósito de 100.00
Saque de 30.50
Saldo insuficiente para sacar 200.00
Saldo de Ana: 69.50
```
hints: Split each line with split(" ") and convert the amount with Number.
sacar must compare the amount with the balance before subtracting, and return true or false.
Use toFixed(2) on every amount you print.

js-09.title: Recursion
js-09.theory:
# Functions that call themselves

A **recursive** function solves a problem by calling itself on a **smaller** version of the same problem. Every recursion needs two parts:

- **Base case**: the simple situation, answered directly, that makes the recursion stop.
- **Recursive step**: shrinks the problem and trusts that the smaller call gives the right answer.

The classic example is the factorial: `n! = n * (n-1)!`, with `0! = 1` (`fatorial` is Portuguese for "factorial"):

```javascript
function fatorial(n) {
  if (n === 0) return 1;          // base case
  return n * fatorial(n - 1);     // recursive step
}
```

## What happens under the hood

Each call is kept on the **call stack**, waiting for the inner call to finish. `fatorial(3)` calls `fatorial(2)`, which calls `fatorial(1)`, which calls `fatorial(0)`. That one returns 1, and the answers come back multiplying: 1, 1, 2, 6.

If the base case is missing (or if the problem doesn't get smaller), the calls never stop and the program overflows the stack (in Node.js and in browsers you get `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded`; in EasyCreator's built-in runner, the message "Recursão profunda demais", meaning "recursion too deep"). The stack has a limit of a few thousand calls, so recursion that goes too deep can fail even when it is correct; in those cases a loop is safer.

## Thinking recursively

The key question is: "if I already knew the answer to a slightly smaller problem, how would I get to the answer to this one?" For example, the sum of the digits of 1234 is the last digit (`1234 % 10 = 4`) plus the sum of the digits of `Math.trunc(1234 / 10) = 123` (`somaDigitos` means "sumDigits"):

```javascript
function somaDigitos(n) {
  if (n < 10) return n;
  return (n % 10) + somaDigitos(Math.trunc(n / 10));
}
```

Each call removes one digit, so the number of calls is the number of digits: the recursion takes about `log10(n)` steps.

## Precision limit

The `number` type only guarantees exact arithmetic with integers up to `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` (2^53 - 1, about 9 × 10^15). `18!` (about 6.4 × 10^15) is still below that limit; `19!` (about 1.2 × 10^17) is already above it, and from there on sums, divisions and remainders may come out rounded. For larger integers, JavaScript has `BigInt` (`20n`), which has no fixed size limit. In this exercise `n` goes up to 18, so `number` is enough.

## Recursion vs. loops

Anything you can do with recursion can be done with loops, and vice versa. Recursion shines on naturally recursive problems (trees, divide and conquer, like the merge sort in the next lesson); a loop usually uses less memory.

## Common mistakes

- A missing or wrong base case (for example, testing `n === 1` and calling it with 0).
- Forgetting the `return` on the recursive call.
- Using `/` without `Math.trunc`: decimals appear (1234 becomes 123.4, then 12.34…) and the sum comes out wrong, with decimal places instead of an integer.
js-09.task:
Write two **recursive** functions (no loops):

- `fatorial(n)` (factorial): returns `n!` (with `0! = 1`);
- `somaDigitos(n)` (sum of digits): returns the sum of the digits of an integer `n ≥ 0`.

Read an integer `n` (0 ≤ n ≤ 18) and print:

```
Fatorial: <n!>
Soma dos dígitos: <sum of the digits of n!>
```

(Fatorial = factorial, Soma dos dígitos = sum of the digits; keep the labels in Portuguese.)

Example: for `5`:

```
Fatorial: 120
Soma dos dígitos: 3
```
hints: fatorial: base case n === 0 returns 1; otherwise n * fatorial(n - 1).
somaDigitos: if n < 10 return n; otherwise (n % 10) + somaDigitos(Math.trunc(n / 10)).

js-10.title: Sorting and binary search
js-10.task:
Read an integer `n` (n ≥ 1), then `n` integers (one per line) and, finally, an integer `alvo` (the target).

1. Sort the numbers in increasing order by **implementing a sorting algorithm yourself** (insertion sort or merge sort; don't use `sort`).
2. Search for `alvo` in the sorted array with **binary search**.

Print:

```
Ordenado: <the sorted numbers separated by spaces>
Posição: <index (starting at 0) of the FIRST occurrence of the target in the sorted array>
```

or, on the second line, `Não encontrado` ("not found") if the target is not in the array.

(Ordenado = sorted, Posição = position; keep the labels in Portuguese.)

Example: for `5`, `8`, `3`, `5`, `1`, `3`, target `5`:

```
Ordenado: 1 3 3 5 8
Posição: 3
```
hints: Start with insertion sort: it's shorter. Test it with negative numbers.
In binary search, use the interval [ini, fim) and move ini to meio + 1 when v[meio] < alvo; otherwise fim = meio.
At the end, the target was found if ini < v.length and v[ini] === alvo.
